full_text:
Interviewer:	The interview’s mainly about the placement and the University’s involvement and some similar stuff to last time, to see how your opinion’s changed since you started work.

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	So, when did you start?

Subject:	I started training on the fifth of September. (Okay) I had two weeks training, then. 

Interviewer:	And you had to start again then? Do you finish in September as well then?

Subject:	I finish in August.

Interviewer:	Okay. Obviously you’re working for the [organisation] but can you tell me a bit about the section that you work in?

Subject:	Okay. I’m working as part of the [name] team. Which is the [name] team. (Okay) And it’s got an awful lot to do with reading processors. (Inaudible).

Interviewer:	It’s supposed to be. Yeah.

Subject:	Yeah the idea is you go to, you go into areas, you take a look at what where doing, and get rid of waste. So we’re there walking about or where there’s tools appropriately used.

Interviewer:	So to make it more efficient and stuff?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Okay, cool. How would you describe the organisation’s attitude to women? 

Subject:	I think they love it. Sort of like a woman bringing something different, I’m not sure.

Interviewer:	Are you the only woman on the team?

Subject:	Yeah. I mean they do sort of make jokes and that. Erm but. They like, their attitude on the whole has been quite good.

Interviewer:	Okay, we’ll talk a little bit more about that later on. How useful do you think that your degree has been so far to the work that you’re do on the placement?

Subject:	I’ve done nothing on my degree. Nothing’s really been of use. Erm I suppose it helps when they do, every so often talk about an engineering problem. Like a couple of weeks ago, they were trying to get a tail-fin on an aircraft, erm down, so they could put some test equipment on it, so they could see the forces and that, when it’s flying. But how to get the tail fin down was a real problem. And they had to work out the angles for the crane, could go out and erm whether it was possible to do it with this crane, or that crane. And they started talking about angles and things like that. I suppose that helps but, no I wouldn’t say it’s been that useful. 

Interviewer:	Is there anything that you wished you had learnt before you started your placement?

Subject:	Not really. I don’t think. No you need to be in the environment, work with the people, to the point somebody tells you. (Yeah) How you, (Inaudible).

Interviewer:	At least it’s experiences then?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Okay, before you started, did the University teach you about health and safety?

Subject:	We just, very few erm lectures on the Health and Safety at Work Act, and how you could get done by the Health and Safety at Work Act, and not really how we should be treated, within that (Inaudible), without saying. 

Interviewer:	Would you have found it useful to have more stuff on that? Is that something that you can learn in the work time?

Subject:	Yeah I think that’s specific to where you are working. (Yeah) Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Okay do you think that University could have done more to prepare you for the placement?

Subject:	Probably not, no. 

Interviewer:	Before you started, did Uni or your department say what they hoped you would get out of the placement at all?

Subject:	Yeah, there was a lot of talk of experience and what you can do, put it on you CV and. Yeah, just experience really. 

Interviewer:	Okay how have you found the transition from education to work? 

Subject:	Yes, it’s been alright. You get the choice as a student whether or not you get up in the morning. Whereas here, you don’t have a choice. If you’re not here, you just get, get a roasting so. Erm and things like, well in this job, you’ve got to polish your shoes. Everything has to be perfect, so you don’t, you know you can’t just roll out of bed, so I suppose that’s been tough, but everything has to be.

Interviewer:	Okay have you had to face any new issues, like office politics or how to get on with the boss and stuff like that?

Subject:	Yeah. There’s a definite rank structure here and you’ve got to be careful what you say to certain people. Erm there’s also like different times where you can have a laugh with people, and then the following day you’ve got to be deadly serious and that. So that’s different and. 

Interviewer:	Is that difficult to get used to or?

Subject:	Yeah. And the first day I walked in, I got told that, ‘Oh by the way this a (Inaudible) somebody she’s put in her, in a equal opportunities case against the [organisation]. Would you sit down and help her write this equal opportunities case?’ And that was on the first day. It was like, ‘Oh my God, what am I all coming into?’ And erm.

Interviewer:	Do you think that was because you were a new student or because you were a woman (inaudible) equal opportunities thing?

Subject:	I think it’s cos … It could have been anything, couldn’t it. I think mainly it is because if I hadn’t had any previous knowledge of this person, so I couldn’t make a judgement. (Yeah) Whereas, and she didn’t want anybody who was previously involved, involved in it this time. So, it worked quite well, but, that was quite daunting, having to take responsibility and take this girl through it, whose older than me. (Yeah) Sit her down and help write an equal opportunities case, who was against the people that had asked me to do it, who are also my bosses.

Interviewer:	Sounds quite scary?

Subject:	 (Inaudible) yeah. 

Interviewer:	Okay how do you feel about going back to Uni when it’s finished?

Subject:	I‘m looking forward to it. Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Do you think it’ll be easy to get back into that type of work again? 

Subject:	I think the, the really sort of academic side of it will be tough, because having not done it for a year, I imagine it will, done it for a year now, and that’ll be difficult. All the fluids and dynamics and maths and all that then. It should be quite easy, I think.

Interviewer:	Okay how do you think that work and Uni differ? Do you think that they have different goals and priorities and values?

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Like what? 

Subject:	Um at Uni you’re only really there for yourself and to get an education and to come away with a piece of paper, telling everyone else that you’ve reached a certain level. Whereas in the workplace, you are working as a group of people, we’ve all got our common aim. 

Interviewer:	Yes, at Uni it’s more about individual.

Subject:	Yeah. Whereas here, if you do something on your own, (inaudible) I guess. 

Interviewer:	Okay does the [organisation] have a structure or programme in place for the placement student?

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	How does that work and what is it, what does it involve?

Subject:	Okay there’s different kind of sections. You’ve got [name], so I’ve, next week I’ve got to down to the [organisation] meeting at [place]. I’ve got history and things like that. And get a taste of that side of things. I’ve got to go on adventure training, two weeks, somewhere. Take some physical thing. We’re told to go on this scheme more or less in January but I’m not too sure about that. Erm for the first few weeks was an introduction. So I went round different areas and got a taster of what they do. I’ve got to do CCS which is (common?) core skills. Which involves basic military er training like, using a gun, using the gas masks, things like that. Although that’s a bit questionable at the minute. 

Interviewer:	Do you think that sort of scheme is a good idea?

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Do you think it could be improved or not? 

Subject:	I think the training at the beginning probably wasn’t enough. Yeah. 

Interviewer:	What else could they do (inaudible)?

Subject:	Well for a, it’s a bit awkward really because you’ve got like half an hour on saluting and, things like that. And all of a sudden you’re dropped in the middle of a place, and I’m getting told off by these guys, for not saluting the right people or saluting somebody I shouldn’t have been. So, things like that (inaudible) can be quite. 

Interviewer:	Okay what does your role involve? Is it what you expected it would be?

Subject:	Okay. Well because of the rank structure, in theory I’ve got five - three guys working under me, on this, in this building, in this team. And I’ve got Wing Commander whose, whose my boss I suppose for this year. And er I go in and lead what they call like an improvement (invent?). And so, I talk to the guys in the area and map the current processes and look at ways to improve them. Erm I have three weeks of data collection. Then take everything out of the room. And I help in re-organising it to flow and (inaudible) and all this kind of good stuff. And then we take data from that process and decide whether or not to improve it. Normally it has by, normally by about a third to fifty percent improvement of what we’re doing efficiency wise. And often there’s a reduction in the required man power as well. So it’s er, I think what I expected was a management role. And I think what I’ve got is a management role. 

Interviewer:	Yeah. How have you found that managing people?

Subject:	Well erm it’s quite scary at first because they all think you know what you’re talking about. But you haven’t a clue. (Inaudible) And you’re just sitting there like yeah don’t know what you’re talking about. But like this morning I went down to one of the areas erm that we’d done an (invent?) of last week. And we’re doing another one in a similar kind of area, in three weeks time. And the guy that’s running it, asked me who his facilitator was going to be. And I said, it’s not going to be me this time, it’s going to be the Wing Commander. And he was like, ‘Oh so Ma’am you’re not coming down to our area then?’ And I was like, ‘No not this time’. Okay, so I felt as if I must have been some kind of use because he were asking me for me back. (Yeah) So that’s all good, so. But it’s just very scary, telling guys that are maybe twenty, thirty years older, have got twenty, thirty years more experience what, what they should be doing. It doesn’t makes sense. 

Interviewer:	Have they been alright with you then, telling them what to do?

Subject:	Yeah. Some of the younger lads were a bit like, you know, whatever. Most of them are alright. 

Interviewer:	Okay, do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility there? 

Subject:	Yeah. There was a push for me to take on more responsibility, but I said I really, couldn’t do it not yet. 

Interviewer:	Yeah. And they were okay with that?

Subject:	Yeah. They wanted me to take on a job that‘s two months ahead of what I am and I’ve not really done the training, because they couldn’t fill the position. So, but I said no so. Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Okay do you feel like they’ve been supportive of you, as far as being a placement student?

Subject:	Yeah. They’ve gone out of their way to make, make it good. To send me places. I’ve been to Italy, I’ve been up to Scotland. Mm, yeah. 

Interviewer:	Okay, how would you summarise the placement so far then?

Subject:	Er, it’s been really good. Erm the learning curve has been you know, straight up. (Yeah) Getting dumped in the, deep end, I think works quite well. I had a couple of weeks, Er a couple of weeks ago actually, where I was like oh my God, this is getting too much, but when I turned around and said, ‘I can’t do this’, they dealt with it, and. 

Interviewer:	Okay what would you say are the best and the worst things so far? 

Subject:	The best thing has been able to get out and about. Going to Italy (Yeah) that was great. Erm. But working with the guys as well is really good. And they start to talk back and give you, give you some feedback (Yeah) that’s good. Sometimes they just sit quiet and just nod and do what you say. But then when you actually start to question why they’re doing that or what, what they’re doing this for? Who told you to do that? And then you start to get more feedback. You know I was working with a guy a couple of weeks ago on concept meetings. And it started off the week, saying ‘Oh I don’t want to get involved with that.’ By the end of the week, we had him designing this system. It was really good seeing him sort of smile at the end of it, and be really impressed with what he’d done. (Yeah) He was showing all the big bosses with loads of stripes, you know, what he did, and he was only little kid - seventeen, eighteen. It was really good. 

Interviewer:	Okay, is there anything that might be the worst thing? 

Subject:	Knowing how to deal with very high ranking officers, seniors. Even if they have a joke with you, you’ve got to be careful of how you react to it back.

Interviewer:	Yes. That’s a bit (inaudible).

Subject:	You know you take a lot of abuse, but you’ve got to be careful what you give out. You know (inaudible).

Interviewer:	Yeah, okay, do you think it’s met your expectations then so far?

Subject:	It’s been good.

Interviewer:	Is there anything that you thought you would achieve but haven’t yet?

Subject:	Not that I can think of.

Interviewer:	Okay, what do you think that you gained from the placement so far then?

Subject:	I think I’ve become more relaxed speaking to people speaking to people that are older than me. And being able to sort of assess a situation quite early on. You know when you go to a meeting, you know who you should be wary of and who’s on your side. 

Interviewer:	Do you think you’ll use what you learnt at all when you go back to University? 

Subject:	No. No. I might say a lot of acronyms when (inaudible) and I mean I’m sure my friends will be like, ‘what the hell’s she on about’. But no I don’t think so.

Interviewer:	Would you recommend people to do a placement then?

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any drawbacks to doing a placement? 

Subject:	Well I know that a lot of my, a few of my friends that are out, in another industries, aren’t having a good time. A lot of them doing jobs that, may be should have been done by admin or given to somebody a bit.

Interviewer:	So they don’t feel like they’ve been given the right sort of responsibility?

Subject:	Yes, they’re not doing engineering jobs. They’re doing graphics or tea making, stuff like that. So you’ve really got to be careful where you end up. 

Interviewer:	Okay are there any other students on placement here?

Subject:	Here? No. There’s five of us around the UK. 

Interviewer:	Yes, do you meet up with them when you do your training things?

Subject:	We went through training together, and we’re meeting up on Monday to go down to London to go on this, (inaudible). So we meet up every so often go, but we have er email contacts and phone numbers for them so.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s an advantage or disadvantage having other students that you can talk to?

Subject:	I think it’s an advantage having other students, to talk to. But, I think being here on our own means that I’ve got to kind of deal with it. (Yeah) And everybody, well. A lot of the people need to know who I am, know who I am, and what I’m doing here. If I’m, those that don’t know that I’m still a student, just respect me just the same as if I was a normal officer. So I think if there was two or three of us, then, it could be pointing the figure, like oh look at them. And there’s two lads that are together down at [place], and they have a shit time of it because they sort of seen as the students who in the corner and they’re not getting talked to as much. Because they‘ve, they‘ve got each other.

Interviewer:	Yes. So do you feel like you’ve been treated more like a permanent member of staff?

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Okay you said that most of the work that you’re doing is team work. How do you think doing team work in the work place compares to doing team work at Uni? 

Subject:	Team working at uni is so artificial. It’s so much. Erm you’re also at Uni trying to juggle other bits of work that are individuals (Yeah) so, some people prioritise their individual work rather than their team work, or the other way around. People’s priorities and that you, you know are different. Whereas at work, everybody’s trying to do the same things, so. And you have to work with the people at work. You can’t choose not to. Whereas at Uni, a lot of people get put in a group and then just decide, ‘Oh I‘m not going do it’, you know ‘I’m just going to do my own thing’ and do nothing as part of the team effort so. At work we have to get on and do it, whereas at Uni you have the choice not to. 

Interviewer:	So would you say its better doing group work at work than at uni? (Yeah) Do you think that part of it is because you have clearer roles for everybody at work than you have at uni?

Subject:	Yeah and there’s a structure. (Yeah) And doing work the Wing Commander will ask me, you know and you get something done, but that doesn’t necessary mean I have to do it. (Yeah) I can ask [name] or [name] or one of the other guys to do it. Erm or if he thinks it’s something that somebody needs some experience, or he’ll go, (inaudible) go up to [name] and. He will sort it out for me, so. Everybody knows what each other strengths are and that in the place, and there’s a boss. So, he can decide whether something needs to be done or not. Whereas at Uni it’s just kind of, ‘Oh what do you reckon?’ (Yeah) Everybody - people either agree or disagree and then if they don’t, go off in huff and (inaudible). You get on with it. 

Interviewer:	Do you think that doing group work is a good idea at uni then or not?

Subject:	Yeah I think we should do more of it, but … 

Interviewer:	How its organised needs to improve?

Subject:	Yeah, it needs to, yeah it needs a change. Cos you have trouble – I was speaking to [name] about this the other day, when he came to visit - we have trouble with er foreign students as well. Cos their culture and mentalities different (Yeah) their way of, thinking’s different. You know a lot of them just don’t participate in group work. So. I think we need to do more of it at uni, and the way in which it’s done needs to be altered. 

Interviewer:	Is there any one in particular that you’ve liked or disliked working with?

Subject:	The boss here’s awkward. Everyone else is great. But this guy’s a, you know he’s a bit of pain. Once (inaudible). He’s one of these that, nobody else can be right and (Or he can’t be wrong?) Yeah, he’s, yeah he’s one of these that, winds everybody up. And he’s only new. He’s been here a couple of weeks after me. And everybody around the station knows who he is and everybody around the station goes, ‘Oh God, he’s your boss’. And I get on with him fine, but when you see him with a group of people and they have a conversation going on and they’re all sort of going, ‘What the hell’, you know, and you have to sit there and feel really embarrassed (Yeah) because some of the shit that comes out his mouth, some of the stuff he comes out with is so ridiculous and out of place and out of touch with people he’s talking to. I mean he’s got very, very strong ideas about this, this technique that we do, its from, its from Japan. Like engineering in Japan. And, but he’s got to remember that most young people don’t know about it, and don’t feel what he feels about it. And he’s not clued up to that at all, because (inaudible). 

Interviewer:	Have you found that difficult learning how to cope with him then?

Subject:	I’ve not found it difficult. Erm no. When you’re in, but with other people it’s difficult to know how to. But all the other guys I get on great.

Interviewer:	Okay have you got a mentor at all?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	What do you think about it, do you think it’s a good idea? 

Subject:	Yeah he’s great. He’s a Squadron Leader, although he’s erm [title] of the Engineering [name]. And he’s just got his Chartered Engineer status. It was last year, and he’s really good, yeah. Definitely.

Interviewer:	What do you think are like the benefits and drawbacks to having a mentor?

Subject:	I think what’s good is he’s in a different department. So he’s not my direct boss. It’s like I can go and to him and say, ‘Oh God, the Wing Commander has been saying this.’ Or, ‘What do you think about this?’ rather than coming to the guy that just told me about it (Yeah) So that’s, that’s really good. Erm I don’t think there is any real disadvantages.

Interviewer:	Okay do you think that like that you have a particular role to play as mentee, if that’s a word? Is there anything that you should or shouldn’t have been doing? 

Subject:	What to these guys or to give them? 

Interviewer:	So within your relationship with your mentor?

Subject:	I’m suppose to keep a weekly record and get him to sign it.

Interviewer:	So do you have to meet him quite regularly then? 

Subject:	Yes, well I see him at lunch and. When I’ve not seen him for a while, he’ll pop in and I’ll, so I see him quite a, quite a lot to be honest.

Interviewer:	Okay. Is there anyone else that you go to for advice at all?

Subject:	Everybody and anybody, depends what it is. I mean if you’re talking babies and love life, [name], across the road, she’s great, she’s, she’s the PA to the main man, man on engineering with. Er she’s great for that kind of thing. (Yes) And then you speak to the guys about your actually work (Yeah) if I haven’t got a clue. Other people in the block if it’s like what do you wear tonight to this function? 

Interviewer:	Okay. Is there anyone that you would regard as your role model?

Subject:	I think my mentor, [name] (inaudible). He’s got very good qualities. 

Interviewer:	What do you think it is about him that makes him a good role model?

Subject:	He’s approachable, and the guys speak to him. And, there’s, there’s a thin line between knowing your guys well but being able to turn around to them and say, ‘You’re not going home tonight are you?’ Erm ‘you’re going to Iraq’ or something like that and being over familiar. And I think he’s got it just right. (Yeah) He can stand, he can stand back or he can get involved. But he never over steps that mark. 

Interviewer:	Okay. Has anyone from the Uni been to visit you yet?

Subject:	What the staff? (Yes) Yeah [name] was here on Tuesday. 

Interviewer:	Did he explain why he was visiting?

Subject:	Yeah, just to see how I was getting on. 

Interviewer:	Okay how long was he here for?

Subject:	He arrived about eleven. We took him for wonder. We then took him for lunch. And we took him for a little bit of a wonder. So I imagine it was about half past two or three o’clock. 

Interviewer:	Okay. Did he speak to your manager as well?

Subject:	Yes. Took him around (inaudible) and spoke to the Wing Commander here.

Interviewer:	Did you know him already?

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Would you be happy to go to him if you had a problem? Or would you go to someone else at uni?

Subject:	If the Uni needed to get involved, I’d probably speak to him and [placement tutor] at the same time. But, yeah that’s probably who I’d speak to thinking about it. 

Interviewer:	You said ‘if the uni had to get involved’, would you try and sort it out through work first?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah definitely.

Interviewer:	Okay do you know if the Uni or here have a complaints procedure if you did have any serious problems?

Subject:	I don’t know. I’ve no idea. I’d probably give [name] or [name] a ring and complain in that way. Er and here. Yeah you. Get to know these different ways depending on what it, what it was.

Interviewer:	Yeah, okay. Are there appropriate facilities for women here?

Subject:	Funny you should say that, because in some hangers, erm the toilets like are miles away because, I don’t know, because they’re like in the offices, where you find most of your women. Whereas there as a, guys toilets on, down the floor. But here, it’s fine. 

Interviewer:	Yes, it’s just in certain areas?

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Okay can you think of any occasions where you feel like, the fact that you’re a woman has determined the outcome to an event or reactions from people?

Subject:	Um, yeah I suppose. But it’s human nature, it’s the culture that makes it that way. I don’t think they do it, I don’t think that, they do up here. And, and I was told at the beginning when I joined this team, somebody said to me, he said, ‘Oh, I’m glad we’ve got a women on this team, there’s been a study and it’s believed that men respond better to women telling them what to do’. Right, and I seem to have got that response in the areas. Like if I go down and tell them something, and they say, ‘Oh yeah, yeah, yeah’. But whereas if one of the guys go down and say, say something, they’re try and argue with them or, you know. It’s, it’s almost a battle, to the guys whereas sort of. 

Interviewer:	And do you feel like being a woman has worked to your advantage? 

Subject:	Yeah. In - in - in this environment. But then again, the other day we were pulling down walls and they were trying to keep me out of the way and, oh no you can’t lift that. Protect me in a physical, physical environment. So.

Interviewer:	How did you react to that then?

Subject:	 (laughs) Er. I did what I thought I could do and even if they said ‘you can’t do that’, I’d be like ‘I’m alright, I’ll do it, I’m alright’. And when I couldn’t, I just stood back and let them do it. You get a bit of abuse now and then but it’s normally a good laugh, as long as you don’t take too (personally?).

Interviewer:	So jokes and stuff is all quite, you feel it’s all quite friendly and …

Subject:	Yeah, yeah. 

Interviewer:	What sort of jokes do they make then?

Subject:	 (laughs) That I need stilts and or being a woman you shouldn’t do that. You should be cleaning up or if I was cleaning the, ‘Oh that’s where you belong’, and all this kind of thing. 

Interviewer:	As we’re watching him doing the hoovering (student’s male colleague is outside office vacuuming)

Subject:	Yeah. Well that’s quite good about it, yeah. 

Interviewer:	Are they like that with each other as well?

Subject:	Yes. 

Interviewer:	Yeah so you don’t, even though the jokes that you might get are about being a woman, you don’t feel like…?

Subject:	No it’s not at all. I mean everybody has a laugh at everybody else and that’s the way everybody deals with it. And I’m sure if you went in to battle it will be even more going on about stuff because that’s the way people deal with it. So yeah. It is. 
Interviewer:	Okay. Do you still want a career in engineering?

Subject:	Yeah I think, so. Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Would you still like to work for the [organisation] when you finish?

Subject:	Um I think so. But I have a couple of issues the past few weeks with them. I don’t think that’s put me off, big time so. 

Interviewer:	Could this placement help you get a job when you finish?

Subject:	Yep. U-hum. As long as I don’t do something really bad. Get arrested. Pretty close last week, but never mind. Erm. 

Interviewer:	That sounds worrying.

Subject:	Yeah so long as I don’t get into a serious trouble erm they’ll offer me a sponsorship for the rest of the Uni, yeah.

Interviewer:	Oh that’s quite good isn’t it? 

Subject:	Placement in, ensure I get the training when I leave. But that’s assuming I’m a good girl between now and then. 

Interviewer:	(inaudible)

Subject:	Probably yeah. 

Interviewer:	Do you have to like sign up for so long and then (inaudible).

Subject:	Yeah I think it’s another what six years. 

Interviewer:	Are you happy to like commit for that long? (inaudible).

Subject:	I think so. And having thought about how long you spend at Uni but er by the time I leave, it would have been six years, in total. I’ve had a good time there, and it’s flown by so it (inaudible). 

Interviewer:	Okay would you still want to get, be involved in like the managerial side? Or would you rather go into something more technical or specialist?

Subject:	No I think I, found where I’m, I’m good at. (Yeah) Yeah I think I quite enjoy, actually a more managerial side of it. 

Interviewer:	Do you think that your career ambitions have changed at all since you’ve been on your placement?

Subject:	No I don’t think so. No. No. 

Interviewer:	Do you think that the placement experience will help you when you start work after Uni if say you didn’t carry on in the [organisation]?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely. The people skills and the responsibilities that I’ve been given are so big compared to what you get in the outside world. If I turned around and said I’ve been in charge of so many guys have run so many (inaudible). And (inaudible). If I hadn’t done it, I wouldn’t have had any experience in that. 

Interviewer:	Yeah. Okay. These are some questions that I asked you last time. What five words would you use to describe the engineering industry in the [organisation]? Or what sort of area (inaudible). 

Subject:	I don’t remember this question.

Interviewer:	See everyone found it really difficult to answer before so now I’m seeing if it’s easier once you’ve been in the industry. But at the minute it doesn’t appear that way.

Subject:	Five words to describe, what?

Interviewer:	Your experience of engineering so far.

Subject:	Huh. I don’t know. 

Interviewer:	Should I tell you what you said last time? You said that it was technical and male orientated. 

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Do you feel, now that you’ve been in the industry, that there are advantages or disadvantages to being a women in engineering? 

Subject:	Yeah, like I said before the (inaudible). 

Interviewer:	 (inaudible). 

Subject:	 [??] I don’t know whether they sort of listen to you or they don’t want to give you any grief because you’re a woman. I’m not sure. They do seem to respond quite well. But then I’m not sure whether the female technicians responded very well to the female engineers telling them or discussing things with them or telling them what to do.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that might be?

Subject:	I don’t know. 

Interviewer:	Do you think it’s because it is mostly males in the environment, that when they come across another woman, they feel threatened or something?

Subject:	Yeah. Again I think it’s human nature or the culture that we‘re brought up in. I don’t think it, they’re are, they’re aware of

Interviewer:	Yeah no one does anything deliberately, it’s just how you’ve been brought up and taught at school and things?

Subject:	I think what we’re used to dealing with a whole lot of men, and you come across another one that’s a bit like a, well what do I have in common with her, because, I can’t treat her the same as all the other guys. (Yeah) Or, well no, your brain instinctively thinks there’s another women. You know it’s like if you walked into a, a room full of really tall person, but one small person there, you’d migrate to the small person. Or you know a - a room full of black men and you know, and there’s a, you know, a - a black woman, you go, you go with her. Or. Yeah it’s. I think your brain takes over and recognises the difference there and it comes out in what you say. 

Interviewer:	Okay do you think that women should or shouldn’t be encouraged or enabled to go into the engineering industry?

Subject:	I think they should have just exactly the same as everybody else I guess.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that there aren’t more women?

Subject:	What I said the last time. British culture, just doesn’t, lend itself to having equal men and women in the engineering. Just. Doesn’t. Doesn’t work. It doesn’t, the schooling’s wrong and the cultures wrong and the mentality of the people’s wrong. 

Interviewer:	That’s everything, thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: The interview’s mainly about the placement and the University’s involvement and some similar stuff to last time, to see how your opinion’s changed since you started work.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So, when did you start?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I started training on the fifth of September. (Okay) I had two weeks training, then.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And you had to start again then? Do you finish in September as well then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I finish in August.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Obviously you’re working for the [organisation] but can you tell me a bit about the section that you work in?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Okay. I’m working as part of the [name] team. Which is the [name] team. (Okay) And it’s got an awful lot to do with reading processors. (Inaudible).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It’s supposed to be. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah the idea is you go to, you go into areas, you take a look at what where doing, and get rid of waste. So we’re there walking about or where there’s tools appropriately used.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So to make it more efficient and stuff?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, cool. How would you describe the organisation’s attitude to women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think they love it. Sort of like a woman bringing something different, I’m not sure.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you the only woman on the team?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I mean they do sort of make jokes and that. Erm but. They like, their attitude on the whole has been quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, we’ll talk a little bit more about that later on. How useful do you think that your degree has been so far to the work that you’re do on the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’ve done nothing on my degree. Nothing’s really been of use. Erm I suppose it helps when they do, every so often talk about an engineering problem. Like a couple of weeks ago, they were trying to get a tail-fin on an aircraft, erm down, so they could put some test equipment on it, so they could see the forces and that, when it’s flying. But how to get the tail fin down was a real problem. And they had to work out the angles for the crane, could go out and erm whether it was possible to do it with this crane, or that crane. And they started talking about angles and things like that. I suppose that helps but, no I wouldn’t say it’s been that useful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anything that you wished you had learnt before you started your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really. I don’t think. No you need to be in the environment, work with the people, to the point somebody tells you. (Yeah) How you, (Inaudible).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: At least it’s experiences then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, before you started, did the University teach you about health and safety?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We just, very few erm lectures on the Health and Safety at Work Act, and how you could get done by the Health and Safety at Work Act, and not really how we should be treated, within that (Inaudible), without saying.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you have found it useful to have more stuff on that? Is that something that you can learn in the work time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah I think that’s specific to where you are working. (Yeah) Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay do you think that University could have done more to prepare you for the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably not, no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Before you started, did Uni or your department say what they hoped you would get out of the placement at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, there was a lot of talk of experience and what you can do, put it on you CV and. Yeah, just experience really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay how have you found the transition from education to work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, it’s been alright. You get the choice as a student whether or not you get up in the morning. Whereas here, you don’t have a choice. If you’re not here, you just get, get a roasting so. Erm and things like, well in this job, you’ve got to polish your shoes. Everything has to be perfect, so you don’t, you know you can’t just roll out of bed, so I suppose that’s been tough, but everything has to be.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay have you had to face any new issues, like office politics or how to get on with the boss and stuff like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. There’s a definite rank structure here and you’ve got to be careful what you say to certain people. Erm there’s also like different times where you can have a laugh with people, and then the following day you’ve got to be deadly serious and that. So that’s different and.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that difficult to get used to or?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. And the first day I walked in, I got told that, ‘Oh by the way this a (Inaudible) somebody she’s put in her, in a equal opportunities case against the [organisation]. Would you sit down and help her write this equal opportunities case?’ And that was on the first day. It was like, ‘Oh my God, what am I all coming into?’ And erm.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that was because you were a new student or because you were a woman (inaudible) equal opportunities thing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s cos … It could have been anything, couldn’t it. I think mainly it is because if I hadn’t had any previous knowledge of this person, so I couldn’t make a judgement. (Yeah) Whereas, and she didn’t want anybody who was previously involved, involved in it this time. So, it worked quite well, but, that was quite daunting, having to take responsibility and take this girl through it, whose older than me. (Yeah) Sit her down and help write an equal opportunities case, who was against the people that had asked me to do it, who are also my bosses.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Sounds quite scary?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: (Inaudible) yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay how do you feel about going back to Uni when it’s finished?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I‘m looking forward to it. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’ll be easy to get back into that type of work again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think the, the really sort of academic side of it will be tough, because having not done it for a year, I imagine it will, done it for a year now, and that’ll be difficult. All the fluids and dynamics and maths and all that then. It should be quite easy, I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay how do you think that work and Uni differ? Do you think that they have different goals and priorities and values?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Like what?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um at Uni you’re only really there for yourself and to get an education and to come away with a piece of paper, telling everyone else that you’ve reached a certain level. Whereas in the workplace, you are working as a group of people, we’ve all got our common aim.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, at Uni it’s more about individual.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Whereas here, if you do something on your own, (inaudible) I guess.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay does the [organisation] have a structure or programme in place for the placement student?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How does that work and what is it, what does it involve?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Okay there’s different kind of sections. You’ve got [name], so I’ve, next week I’ve got to down to the [organisation] meeting at [place]. I’ve got history and things like that. And get a taste of that side of things. I’ve got to go on adventure training, two weeks, somewhere. Take some physical thing. We’re told to go on this scheme more or less in January but I’m not too sure about that. Erm for the first few weeks was an introduction. So I went round different areas and got a taster of what they do. I’ve got to do CCS which is (common?) core skills. Which involves basic military er training like, using a gun, using the gas masks, things like that. Although that’s a bit questionable at the minute.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that sort of scheme is a good idea?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it could be improved or not?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think the training at the beginning probably wasn’t enough. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What else could they do (inaudible)?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well for a, it’s a bit awkward really because you’ve got like half an hour on saluting and, things like that. And all of a sudden you’re dropped in the middle of a place, and I’m getting told off by these guys, for not saluting the right people or saluting somebody I shouldn’t have been. So, things like that (inaudible) can be quite.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay what does your role involve? Is it what you expected it would be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Okay. Well because of the rank structure, in theory I’ve got five - three guys working under me, on this, in this building, in this team. And I’ve got Wing Commander whose, whose my boss I suppose for this year. And er I go in and lead what they call like an improvement (invent?). And so, I talk to the guys in the area and map the current processes and look at ways to improve them. Erm I have three weeks of data collection. Then take everything out of the room. And I help in re-organising it to flow and (inaudible) and all this kind of good stuff. And then we take data from that process and decide whether or not to improve it. Normally it has by, normally by about a third to fifty percent improvement of what we’re doing efficiency wise. And often there’s a reduction in the required man power as well. So it’s er, I think what I expected was a management role. And I think what I’ve got is a management role.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. How have you found that managing people?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well erm it’s quite scary at first because they all think you know what you’re talking about. But you haven’t a clue. (Inaudible) And you’re just sitting there like yeah don’t know what you’re talking about. But like this morning I went down to one of the areas erm that we’d done an (invent?) of last week. And we’re doing another one in a similar kind of area, in three weeks time. And the guy that’s running it, asked me who his facilitator was going to be. And I said, it’s not going to be me this time, it’s going to be the Wing Commander. And he was like, ‘Oh so Ma’am you’re not coming down to our area then?’ And I was like, ‘No not this time’. Okay, so I felt as if I must have been some kind of use because he were asking me for me back. (Yeah) So that’s all good, so. But it’s just very scary, telling guys that are maybe twenty, thirty years older, have got twenty, thirty years more experience what, what they should be doing. It doesn’t makes sense.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have they been alright with you then, telling them what to do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Some of the younger lads were a bit like, you know, whatever. Most of them are alright.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility there?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. There was a push for me to take on more responsibility, but I said I really, couldn’t do it not yet.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. And they were okay with that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. They wanted me to take on a job that‘s two months ahead of what I am and I’ve not really done the training, because they couldn’t fill the position. So, but I said no so. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay do you feel like they’ve been supportive of you, as far as being a placement student?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. They’ve gone out of their way to make, make it good. To send me places. I’ve been to Italy, I’ve been up to Scotland. Mm, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, how would you summarise the placement so far then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, it’s been really good. Erm the learning curve has been you know, straight up. (Yeah) Getting dumped in the, deep end, I think works quite well. I had a couple of weeks, Er a couple of weeks ago actually, where I was like oh my God, this is getting too much, but when I turned around and said, ‘I can’t do this’, they dealt with it, and.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay what would you say are the best and the worst things so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The best thing has been able to get out and about. Going to Italy (Yeah) that was great. Erm. But working with the guys as well is really good. And they start to talk back and give you, give you some feedback (Yeah) that’s good. Sometimes they just sit quiet and just nod and do what you say. But then when you actually start to question why they’re doing that or what, what they’re doing this for? Who told you to do that? And then you start to get more feedback. You know I was working with a guy a couple of weeks ago on concept meetings. And it started off the week, saying ‘Oh I don’t want to get involved with that.’ By the end of the week, we had him designing this system. It was really good seeing him sort of smile at the end of it, and be really impressed with what he’d done. (Yeah) He was showing all the big bosses with loads of stripes, you know, what he did, and he was only little kid - seventeen, eighteen. It was really good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, is there anything that might be the worst thing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Knowing how to deal with very high ranking officers, seniors. Even if they have a joke with you, you’ve got to be careful of how you react to it back.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes. That’s a bit (inaudible).

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: You know you take a lot of abuse, but you’ve got to be careful what you give out. You know (inaudible).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, okay, do you think it’s met your expectations then so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s been good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anything that you thought you would achieve but haven’t yet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not that I can think of.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, what do you think that you gained from the placement so far then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think I’ve become more relaxed speaking to people speaking to people that are older than me. And being able to sort of assess a situation quite early on. You know when you go to a meeting, you know who you should be wary of and who’s on your side.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think you’ll use what you learnt at all when you go back to University?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. No. I might say a lot of acronyms when (inaudible) and I mean I’m sure my friends will be like, ‘what the hell’s she on about’. But no I don’t think so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you recommend people to do a placement then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are any drawbacks to doing a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well I know that a lot of my, a few of my friends that are out, in another industries, aren’t having a good time. A lot of them doing jobs that, may be should have been done by admin or given to somebody a bit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So they don’t feel like they’ve been given the right sort of responsibility?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, they’re not doing engineering jobs. They’re doing graphics or tea making, stuff like that. So you’ve really got to be careful where you end up.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay are there any other students on placement here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Here? No. There’s five of us around the UK.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, do you meet up with them when you do your training things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We went through training together, and we’re meeting up on Monday to go down to London to go on this, (inaudible). So we meet up every so often go, but we have er email contacts and phone numbers for them so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s an advantage or disadvantage having other students that you can talk to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s an advantage having other students, to talk to. But, I think being here on our own means that I’ve got to kind of deal with it. (Yeah) And everybody, well. A lot of the people need to know who I am, know who I am, and what I’m doing here. If I’m, those that don’t know that I’m still a student, just respect me just the same as if I was a normal officer. So I think if there was two or three of us, then, it could be pointing the figure, like oh look at them. And there’s two lads that are together down at [place], and they have a shit time of it because they sort of seen as the students who in the corner and they’re not getting talked to as much. Because they‘ve, they‘ve got each other.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes. So do you feel like you’ve been treated more like a permanent member of staff?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay you said that most of the work that you’re doing is team work. How do you think doing team work in the work place compares to doing team work at Uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Team working at uni is so artificial. It’s so much. Erm you’re also at Uni trying to juggle other bits of work that are individuals (Yeah) so, some people prioritise their individual work rather than their team work, or the other way around. People’s priorities and that you, you know are different. Whereas at work, everybody’s trying to do the same things, so. And you have to work with the people at work. You can’t choose not to. Whereas at Uni, a lot of people get put in a group and then just decide, ‘Oh I‘m not going do it’, you know ‘I’m just going to do my own thing’ and do nothing as part of the team effort so. At work we have to get on and do it, whereas at Uni you have the choice not to.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So would you say its better doing group work at work than at uni? (Yeah) Do you think that part of it is because you have clearer roles for everybody at work than you have at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah and there’s a structure. (Yeah) And doing work the Wing Commander will ask me, you know and you get something done, but that doesn’t necessary mean I have to do it. (Yeah) I can ask [name] or [name] or one of the other guys to do it. Erm or if he thinks it’s something that somebody needs some experience, or he’ll go, (inaudible) go up to [name] and. He will sort it out for me, so. Everybody knows what each other strengths are and that in the place, and there’s a boss. So, he can decide whether something needs to be done or not. Whereas at Uni it’s just kind of, ‘Oh what do you reckon?’ (Yeah) Everybody - people either agree or disagree and then if they don’t, go off in huff and (inaudible). You get on with it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that doing group work is a good idea at uni then or not?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah I think we should do more of it, but …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How its organised needs to improve?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it needs to, yeah it needs a change. Cos you have trouble – I was speaking to [name] about this the other day, when he came to visit - we have trouble with er foreign students as well. Cos their culture and mentalities different (Yeah) their way of, thinking’s different. You know a lot of them just don’t participate in group work. So. I think we need to do more of it at uni, and the way in which it’s done needs to be altered.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there any one in particular that you’ve liked or disliked working with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The boss here’s awkward. Everyone else is great. But this guy’s a, you know he’s a bit of pain. Once (inaudible). He’s one of these that, nobody else can be right and (Or he can’t be wrong?) Yeah, he’s, yeah he’s one of these that, winds everybody up. And he’s only new. He’s been here a couple of weeks after me. And everybody around the station knows who he is and everybody around the station goes, ‘Oh God, he’s your boss’. And I get on with him fine, but when you see him with a group of people and they have a conversation going on and they’re all sort of going, ‘What the hell’, you know, and you have to sit there and feel really embarrassed (Yeah) because some of the shit that comes out his mouth, some of the stuff he comes out with is so ridiculous and out of place and out of touch with people he’s talking to. I mean he’s got very, very strong ideas about this, this technique that we do, its from, its from Japan. Like engineering in Japan. And, but he’s got to remember that most young people don’t know about it, and don’t feel what he feels about it. And he’s not clued up to that at all, because (inaudible).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you found that difficult learning how to cope with him then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’ve not found it difficult. Erm no. When you’re in, but with other people it’s difficult to know how to. But all the other guys I get on great.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay have you got a mentor at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think about it, do you think it’s a good idea?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah he’s great. He’s a Squadron Leader, although he’s erm [title] of the Engineering [name]. And he’s just got his Chartered Engineer status. It was last year, and he’s really good, yeah. Definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think are like the benefits and drawbacks to having a mentor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think what’s good is he’s in a different department. So he’s not my direct boss. It’s like I can go and to him and say, ‘Oh God, the Wing Commander has been saying this.’ Or, ‘What do you think about this?’ rather than coming to the guy that just told me about it (Yeah) So that’s, that’s really good. Erm I don’t think there is any real disadvantages.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay do you think that like that you have a particular role to play as mentee, if that’s a word? Is there anything that you should or shouldn’t have been doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: What to these guys or to give them?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So within your relationship with your mentor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m suppose to keep a weekly record and get him to sign it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So do you have to meet him quite regularly then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, well I see him at lunch and. When I’ve not seen him for a while, he’ll pop in and I’ll, so I see him quite a, quite a lot to be honest.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Is there anyone else that you go to for advice at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Everybody and anybody, depends what it is. I mean if you’re talking babies and love life, [name], across the road, she’s great, she’s, she’s the PA to the main man, man on engineering with. Er she’s great for that kind of thing. (Yes) And then you speak to the guys about your actually work (Yeah) if I haven’t got a clue. Other people in the block if it’s like what do you wear tonight to this function?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Is there anyone that you would regard as your role model?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think my mentor, [name] (inaudible). He’s got very good qualities.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think it is about him that makes him a good role model?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: He’s approachable, and the guys speak to him. And, there’s, there’s a thin line between knowing your guys well but being able to turn around to them and say, ‘You’re not going home tonight are you?’ Erm ‘you’re going to Iraq’ or something like that and being over familiar. And I think he’s got it just right. (Yeah) He can stand, he can stand back or he can get involved. But he never over steps that mark.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Has anyone from the Uni been to visit you yet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: What the staff? (Yes) Yeah [name] was here on Tuesday.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did he explain why he was visiting?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, just to see how I was getting on.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay how long was he here for?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: He arrived about eleven. We took him for wonder. We then took him for lunch. And we took him for a little bit of a wonder. So I imagine it was about half past two or three o’clock.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Did he speak to your manager as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. Took him around (inaudible) and spoke to the Wing Commander here.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you know him already?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you be happy to go to him if you had a problem? Or would you go to someone else at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: If the Uni needed to get involved, I’d probably speak to him and [placement tutor] at the same time. But, yeah that’s probably who I’d speak to thinking about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You said ‘if the uni had to get involved’, would you try and sort it out through work first?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay do you know if the Uni or here have a complaints procedure if you did have any serious problems?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know. I’ve no idea. I’d probably give [name] or [name] a ring and complain in that way. Er and here. Yeah you. Get to know these different ways depending on what it, what it was.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, okay. Are there appropriate facilities for women here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Funny you should say that, because in some hangers, erm the toilets like are miles away because, I don’t know, because they’re like in the offices, where you find most of your women. Whereas there as a, guys toilets on, down the floor. But here, it’s fine.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, it’s just in certain areas?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay can you think of any occasions where you feel like, the fact that you’re a woman has determined the outcome to an event or reactions from people?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, yeah I suppose. But it’s human nature, it’s the culture that makes it that way. I don’t think they do it, I don’t think that, they do up here. And, and I was told at the beginning when I joined this team, somebody said to me, he said, ‘Oh, I’m glad we’ve got a women on this team, there’s been a study and it’s believed that men respond better to women telling them what to do’. Right, and I seem to have got that response in the areas. Like if I go down and tell them something, and they say, ‘Oh yeah, yeah, yeah’. But whereas if one of the guys go down and say, say something, they’re try and argue with them or, you know. It’s, it’s almost a battle, to the guys whereas sort of.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And do you feel like being a woman has worked to your advantage?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. In - in - in this environment. But then again, the other day we were pulling down walls and they were trying to keep me out of the way and, oh no you can’t lift that. Protect me in a physical, physical environment. So.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you react to that then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: (laughs) Er. I did what I thought I could do and even if they said ‘you can’t do that’, I’d be like ‘I’m alright, I’ll do it, I’m alright’. And when I couldn’t, I just stood back and let them do it. You get a bit of abuse now and then but it’s normally a good laugh, as long as you don’t take too (personally?).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So jokes and stuff is all quite, you feel it’s all quite friendly and …

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What sort of jokes do they make then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: (laughs) That I need stilts and or being a woman you shouldn’t do that. You should be cleaning up or if I was cleaning the, ‘Oh that’s where you belong’, and all this kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: As we’re watching him doing the hoovering (student’s male colleague is outside office vacuuming)

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Well that’s quite good about it, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they like that with each other as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah so you don’t, even though the jokes that you might get are about being a woman, you don’t feel like…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No it’s not at all. I mean everybody has a laugh at everybody else and that’s the way everybody deals with it. And I’m sure if you went in to battle it will be even more going on about stuff because that’s the way people deal with it. So yeah. It is.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you still want a career in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah I think, so. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you still like to work for the [organisation] when you finish?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um I think so. But I have a couple of issues the past few weeks with them. I don’t think that’s put me off, big time so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Could this placement help you get a job when you finish?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yep. U-hum. As long as I don’t do something really bad. Get arrested. Pretty close last week, but never mind. Erm.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That sounds worrying.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah so long as I don’t get into a serious trouble erm they’ll offer me a sponsorship for the rest of the Uni, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Oh that’s quite good isn’t it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Placement in, ensure I get the training when I leave. But that’s assuming I’m a good girl between now and then.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: (inaudible)

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you have to like sign up for so long and then (inaudible).

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah I think it’s another what six years.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you happy to like commit for that long? (inaudible).

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so. And having thought about how long you spend at Uni but er by the time I leave, it would have been six years, in total. I’ve had a good time there, and it’s flown by so it (inaudible).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay would you still want to get, be involved in like the managerial side? Or would you rather go into something more technical or specialist?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No I think I, found where I’m, I’m good at. (Yeah) Yeah I think I quite enjoy, actually a more managerial side of it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that your career ambitions have changed at all since you’ve been on your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No I don’t think so. No. No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the placement experience will help you when you start work after Uni if say you didn’t carry on in the [organisation]?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely. The people skills and the responsibilities that I’ve been given are so big compared to what you get in the outside world. If I turned around and said I’ve been in charge of so many guys have run so many (inaudible). And (inaudible). If I hadn’t done it, I wouldn’t have had any experience in that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Okay. These are some questions that I asked you last time. What five words would you use to describe the engineering industry in the [organisation]? Or what sort of area (inaudible).

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t remember this question.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: See everyone found it really difficult to answer before so now I’m seeing if it’s easier once you’ve been in the industry. But at the minute it doesn’t appear that way.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Five words to describe, what?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Your experience of engineering so far.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Huh. I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Should I tell you what you said last time? You said that it was technical and male orientated.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel, now that you’ve been in the industry, that there are advantages or disadvantages to being a women in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, like I said before the (inaudible).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: (inaudible).

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: [??] I don’t know whether they sort of listen to you or they don’t want to give you any grief because you’re a woman. I’m not sure. They do seem to respond quite well. But then I’m not sure whether the female technicians responded very well to the female engineers telling them or discussing things with them or telling them what to do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that might be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’s because it is mostly males in the environment, that when they come across another woman, they feel threatened or something?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Again I think it’s human nature or the culture that we‘re brought up in. I don’t think it, they’re are, they’re aware of

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah no one does anything deliberately, it’s just how you’ve been brought up and taught at school and things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think what we’re used to dealing with a whole lot of men, and you come across another one that’s a bit like a, well what do I have in common with her, because, I can’t treat her the same as all the other guys. (Yeah) Or, well no, your brain instinctively thinks there’s another women. You know it’s like if you walked into a, a room full of really tall person, but one small person there, you’d migrate to the small person. Or you know a - a room full of black men and you know, and there’s a, you know, a - a black woman, you go, you go with her. Or. Yeah it’s. I think your brain takes over and recognises the difference there and it comes out in what you say.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay do you think that women should or shouldn’t be encouraged or enabled to go into the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think they should have just exactly the same as everybody else I guess.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that there aren’t more women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: What I said the last time. British culture, just doesn’t, lend itself to having equal men and women in the engineering. Just. Doesn’t. Doesn’t work. It doesn’t, the schooling’s wrong and the cultures wrong and the mentality of the people’s wrong.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s everything, thank you very much.
